title: The Wall Street Game and the Community Game
text:
Lee Ross of Stanford, with Varda Liberman and Steven Samuels, wanted to compare two forces that might decide whether people cooperate: their personal character, or the way the situation is described to them.

They asked dormitory advisers at Stanford to nominate students they thought were especially likely to cooperate or especially likely to compete. The nominated students then played a version of the prisoner's dilemma, a game in which each player chooses to cooperate or defect. Mutual cooperation pays both well, but each player can earn more by defecting while the other cooperates.

The game was exactly the same for everyone. The only difference was its name. Half the pairs were told they were playing the Wall Street Game; the other half, the Community Game.

The label had a large effect. In the Community Game, about two thirds of players cooperated in the first round, and cooperation stayed high. In the Wall Street Game, only about a third did. The advisers' predictions, based on knowing the students personally, made little difference to what they did. A follow-up with Israeli participants found a similar pattern. Calling the same game by a different name changed what players expected from each other, and so what they chose.
lesson: How you frame a joint task sets how people play it. Describe your team's work as a shared effort, not a contest, and people tend to act accordingly.
people: Varda Liberman, Steven Samuels, Lee Ross
location: Stanford University, Stanford, USA, and Israel
source: Liberman, V., Samuels, S. M., and Ross, L. (2004). The name of the game: Predictive power of reputations versus situational labels in determining prisoner's dilemma game moves. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 30(9), 1175-1185.
